entries.1.1: When Rama had won back the kingdom and the rakshasas had been destroyed, all the sages came to greet Raghava.
entries.1.2: Kaushika, Yavakrita, Gargya, Galava, and Kanva the son of Medhatithi — these who dwelt in the eastern quarter.
entries.1.3: Svastyatreya, the venerable Namuchi and Pramuchi — these came together with Agastya, who dwelt in the southern quarter.
entries.1.4: Nrishadgu, Kavasha, Dhaumya and the great sage Raudreya — these too came with their disciples, who dwelt in the western quarter.
entries.1.5: Vasishtha, Kashyapa, Atri, Vishvamitra with Gautama, Jamadagni and Bharadvaja — these, the seven sages, came as well.
entries.1.6: These seven have their dwelling always in the northern quarter.
entries.1.7: Those great souls reached Raghava's palace and waited at the gate, radiant as the sacrificial fire, learned in the Vedas and their branches and skilled in many sciences.
entries.1.8: Agastya, best among sages and devoted to dharma, said to the gatekeeper, 'Announce to the son of Dasaratha that we sages have come.'
entries.1.9: At Agastya's word the gatekeeper went swiftly and entered at once into the presence of the great-souled Raghava.
entries.1.10: He was skilled in reading intent, of good conduct, capable and steady. Seeing Rama before him, radiant as the full moon,
entries.1.11: he told him that Agastya had arrived together with the sages.
entries.1.12: Hearing that the sages had come, bright as the rising sun, Rama answered the gatekeeper, 'Bring them in, and let them be at their ease.'
entries.1.13: Seeing the sages arrived, he rose to meet them with joined palms, honoured them with water for the feet and the guest-offering, and respectfully presented a cow.
entries.1.14: Rama saluted them and with care appointed them seats — great and excellent seats worked with gold,
entries.1.15: spread with kusha grass and covered over with deerskin. The bulls among sages took those seats, each as befitted him.
entries.1.16: When Rama had asked after their welfare, the great sages learned in the Vedas, with their disciples and their leaders, spoke to him.
entries.1.17: 'All is well with us everywhere, mighty-armed delight of the Raghus. By good fortune we see you in health, with your enemies destroyed.
entries.1.18: 'By good fortune, king, Ravana who made the worlds cry out has fallen to you. Ravana with his sons and grandsons was no burden to you, Rama.
entries.1.19: 'With your bow you could conquer the three worlds, and of that there is no doubt. By good fortune, Rama, Ravana lord of the rakshasas has been slain by you.
entries.1.20: 'By good fortune we see you victorious today, together with Sita, and with Lakshmana your brother, devoted to dharma, who works always for your good.
entries.1.21: 'Today we see you, king, with your mothers and your brothers about you. By good fortune Prahasta, Vikata, Virupaksha, Mahodara and the unassailable Akampana — those night-rangers — have all been slain.
entries.1.22: 'By good fortune, Rama, Kumbhakarna was brought down by you in battle — he whose bulk had no measure to match it in this world.
entries.1.23: 'By good fortune, Rama, Trishiras and Atikaya, Devantaka and Narantaka, night-rangers of great valour, fell to you.
entries.1.24: 'By good fortune, Rama, Kumbha and Nikumbha, those two rakshasas terrible to behold, the sons of Kumbhakarna, were slain in the fray.
entries.1.25: 'Yuddhonmatta and Matta, who were as Yama the ender at the closing of an age, and mighty Yajnakopa, and the rakshasa named Dhumraksha —
entries.1.26: 'these masters of weapon and missile, who wrought a dreadful slaughter, were by good fortune destroyed by your arrows, which were death itself in form.
entries.1.27: 'By good fortune you met the lord of the rakshasas in single combat and took the victory from one whom the gods themselves could not slay.
entries.1.28: 'In that battle Ravana met no defeat at any other hand. By good fortune, when Ravana's son came to single combat, he was slain by you.
entries.1.29: 'By good fortune, mighty-armed hero, you were delivered from that enemy of the gods who bore down upon you like death, and the victory was yours.
entries.1.30: 'We all rejoice with you, having heard of Indrajit's death. In battle he could not be slain by any living being, master as he was of great illusion.
entries.1.31: 'This indeed is our wonder — that we should hear Indrajit had been slain.
entries.1.32: 'These and many other rakshasas who took what form they pleased — by good fortune those heroes were slain by you, increaser of the line of the Raghus.
entries.1.33: 'Having granted this holy and gracious gift of safety, hero, by good fortune you flourish in victory, Kakutstha, wearer-down of foes.'
entries.1.34: Hearing the words of those sages of disciplined soul, Rama was filled with the greatest wonder and spoke with joined palms.
entries.1.35: 'Venerable ones, passing over Kumbhakarna and Ravana the night-ranger, both of great valour, why is it Ravana's son whom you praise?
entries.1.36: 'Mahodara, Prahasta, the rakshasa Virupaksha, Matta and Unmatta both unassailable, Devantaka and Narantaka —
entries.1.37: 'passing over these men of great valour, why is it Ravana's son whom you praise?
entries.1.38: 'Atikaya, Trishiras and Dhumraksha the night-ranger — passing over these men of great valour, why is it Ravana's son whom you praise?
entries.1.39: 'What was his power, what his strength, what his prowess? For what reason does he surpass Ravana himself?
entries.1.40: 'If it may be heard by me — and I do not command you — if it is no secret that may not be told, I wish to hear it. Let it be spoken.
entries.1.41: 'How was even Shakra conquered by him, and how did he obtain his boon? How was the son so strong, and not his father Ravana?
entries.1.42: 'How was he greater than his father, and how did that rakshasa conquer Shakra in the great battle? Tell me today what boons he won — tell me all of it, lord of sages, since I ask you.'
entries.2.1: Hearing those words of the great-souled Raghava, the pot-born sage of great splendour spoke thus to Rama.
entries.2.2: 'Listen, Rama, to the tale of his great might and strength — by which he slew his enemies, and by which he could not be slain by them.
entries.2.3: 'First I shall tell you Ravana's lineage and his birth, Raghava, and the boon that was granted to him.
entries.2.4: 'Long ago in the Krita age, Rama, there was a lord who was the son of Prajapati, a brahmarshi named Pulastya, like the Grandsire himself made visible.
entries.2.5: 'His qualities of dharma and of conduct cannot be recounted. It is enough to say that he was called the son of Prajapati.
entries.2.6: 'Being Prajapati's son he was dear to the gods, and that great-minded one delighted the whole world with his shining virtues.
entries.2.7: 'Following the path of dharma, that bull among sages went to the hermitage of Trinabindu on the slope of the great mountain Meru, and dwelt there.
entries.2.8: 'That soul of dharma performed austerities, his senses restrained and given to the study of the sacred texts. But maidens came to his hermitage and disturbed him.
entries.2.9: 'Daughters of gods and of serpents, and daughters of royal sages, and apsaras at their play, came to that place.
entries.2.10: 'Because it was fit for enjoyment in every season and because the woodland was beautiful, the maidens came there always and played.
entries.2.11: 'Because the place where the twice-born Pulastya dwelt was so lovely, those blameless ones singing, playing on instruments and dancing disturbed the austerities of that ascetic.
entries.2.12: 'Then that great sage of mighty splendour grew angry and declared, "Whichever of them comes within my sight shall conceive."
entries.2.13: 'All of them heard the word of that great soul, and fearing the curse of a brahmin they came no more to that place.
entries.2.14: 'But the daughter of the royal sage Trinabindu did not hear it.
entries.2.15: 'She went to the hermitage and wandered there without fear. Standing there she saw none of her companions come.
entries.2.16: 'At that hour the great sage born of Prajapati, of mighty splendour, was reciting the sacred texts, made luminous by his own austerity.
entries.2.17: 'And she, hearing the sound of the Veda and seeing that treasury of penance, grew pale of body and showed the signs of conception.
entries.2.18: 'Seeing that change in herself she was troubled, and thinking "What is this that has come upon me?" she went and stood in her father's hermitage.
entries.2.19: 'Seeing her in that state Trinabindu said, "Why do you bear a form so unlike yourself?"
entries.2.20: 'Then the maiden, downcast, joined her palms and said to the ascetic, "Father, I do not know the cause by which my form has become like this.
entries.2.21: '"Only that I went alone before to the divine hermitage of that great sage of disciplined soul, Pulastya, seeking my companions,
entries.2.22: '"and I saw none of them come there. Seeing this change in my form, I came here in fear."
entries.2.23: 'Then the royal sage Trinabindu, whose radiance was kindled by austerity, entered into meditation, and saw that this was the sage's doing.
entries.2.24: 'Understanding the curse of that great sage of disciplined soul, he took his daughter and went and said this to Pulastya.
entries.2.25: '"Venerable one, take this my daughter, adorned with her own virtues, as an offering — she who has come of her own accord, great sage.
entries.2.26: '"To you who are engaged in austerity, whose senses are worn with effort, she will be ever devoted in service, and of that there is no doubt."
entries.2.27: 'To the righteous royal sage who spoke those words the twice-born answered "So be it," willing to receive the maiden.
entries.2.28: 'Having given her in due form, he returned to his own hermitage. And she dwelt there, pleasing her husband with her virtues.
entries.2.29: 'That bull among sages was pleased with her conduct and character, and being pleased, that one of great splendour spoke these words.
entries.2.30: '"I am well satisfied, fair one, with the abundance of your virtues. Therefore, lady, I grant you today a son equal to myself,
entries.2.31: '"who shall carry forward both our lines and be known as the son of Pulastya. And because you heard me as I recited the Veda,
entries.2.32: '"he shall be named Vishrava, and of that there is no doubt." Being told this, that lady with a heart full of joy
entries.2.33: 'in no long time bore a son, Vishrava, renowned in the three worlds and possessed of fame and righteousness.
entries.2.34: 'Learned in scripture, even-eyed toward all, devoted to vows and observances, the sage Vishrava came to be endowed with austerity like his father.'
entries.2.35: Thus ends the second canto of the Uttara Kanda in the Ramayana, the first poem, composed by the sage Valmiki.
entries.2.43: Thus ends the first canto of the Uttara Kanda in the Ramayana, the first poem, composed by the sage Valmiki.
entries.3.1: 'Then Vishrava, the son of Pulastya and a bull among sages, in no long time stood firm in austerity like his father.
entries.3.2: 'He was truthful, of good character, tranquil, given to the study of the sacred texts, pure, unattached to all enjoyments and ever devoted to dharma.
entries.3.3: 'Knowing his manner of life, the great sage Bharadvaja gave his own daughter Devavarnini to Vishrava as wife.
entries.3.4: 'Receiving Bharadvaja's daughter in due form, and considering with a mind turned toward offspring what would be best,
entries.3.5: 'Vishrava, that bull among sages, filled with the highest joy, begot upon her a child of surpassing wonder, endowed with strength,
entries.3.6: 'and possessed of every brahminical virtue — so that knower of dharma became a father. At his birth the Grandsire was delighted,
entries.3.7: 'and seeing that his mind was set on what was good, he said, 'He shall be the lord of wealth.' Then, pleased, he gave him a name in the presence of the divine sages.
entries.3.8: '"Since he is the child of Vishrava and resembles Vishrava himself, let him be renowned by the name Vaishravana."
entries.3.9: 'And Vaishravana, dwelling there in the forest of penance, grew in mighty splendour like the fire that is fed with oblations.
entries.3.10: 'While he stayed in that hermitage this thought arose in the great soul: 'I shall practise the highest dharma, for dharma is the highest goal.'
entries.3.11: 'For a thousand years he performed austerity in that great forest, bound by fierce observances, and did great penance.
entries.3.12: 'When each thousand years was complete he took up a new discipline — living on water, then on air alone, then taking nothing at all.
entries.3.13: 'Thus thousands of years passed as though they were a single year. Then Brahma of great splendour, well pleased, came with the hosts of the gods and Indra among them,
entries.3.14: 'and going to his hermitage said these words: 'I am satisfied with you, child, for this work of yours, faithful to your vows. Choose a boon; may it be well with you, for you are worthy of a boon, great-minded one.'
entries.3.15: 'Then Vaishravana said to the Grandsire who stood before him, 'Lord, I would wish for the guardianship of a quarter of the world, and the keeping of wealth.'
entries.3.16: 'Then Brahma, with a heart well pleased, answered Vaishravana gladly, together with the hosts of the gods: 'So be it.
entries.3.17: '"I am even now minded to create a fourth among the guardians of the world.
entries.3.18: '"The station you desire is that of Yama, Indra and Varuna. Go then, knower of dharma, and attain the lordship of the treasures. You shall be the fourth beside Shakra, Varuna and Yama.
entries.3.19: '"And receive this chariot named Pushpaka, bright as the sun, to bear you; become the equal of the gods.
entries.3.20: '"May it be well with you. We shall all go as we came. We are fulfilled, dear child, having given you these two boons."
entries.3.21: 'Having spoken thus, Brahma went with the gods to his own abode.
entries.3.22: 'When Brahma and the gods had gone up into the sky, he went to his father in the forest and said with joined palms, his soul composed, 'The god Prajapati has not appointed me a dwelling.
entries.3.23: '"Venerable one, I have obtained the boon I desired from the Grandsire. Look now, lord, and find me some fitting place to dwell,
entries.3.24: '"where no living creature of any kind may suffer hurt." Being addressed thus by his son, Vishrava, that bull among sages,
entries.3.25: 'knower of dharma and best of the good, spoke these words: 'Listen. On the shore of the southern ocean there is a mountain named Trikuta.
entries.3.26: '"On its summit stands a great city like the city of Mahendra — the lovely city named Lanka, built by Vishvakarma
entries.3.27: '"for the rakshasas to dwell in, as Amaravati was built for Indra. Dwell there, and may it be well with you; there is no doubt in this.
entries.3.28: '"Its ramparts and bars are of gold, it is furnished with engines and weapons, and it is a lovely city with archways of gold and beryl.
entries.3.29: '"It was abandoned long ago by the rakshasas, who were driven by fear of Vishnu; it lies empty, all the hosts of rakshasas having gone down to the nether world.
entries.3.30: '"Lanka stands empty now and has no lord. Go there then, my son, and dwell at your ease.
entries.3.31: '"Your dwelling there will be blameless, and no creature will be troubled by it." Hearing this most righteous word of his father,
entries.3.32: 'that soul of dharma made his dwelling in Lanka upon the mountain's crest, together with thousands of nairritas glad and rejoicing.
entries.3.33: 'And in no long time the city was filled at his command.
entries.3.34: 'That soul of dharma, the bull among nairritas and son of Vishrava, dwelt there in contentment, in Lanka girded about by the sea.
entries.3.35: 'And from time to time that righteous lord of wealth came in the Pushpaka, humble of spirit, to visit his father and his mother.
entries.3.36: 'Praised by the hosts of gods and gandharvas, his dwelling adorned by the dancing of apsaras, that keeper of wealth went to his father's presence, shining like the sun with its rays.'
entries.3.37: Thus ends the third canto of the Uttara Kanda in the Ramayana, the first poem, composed by the sage Valmiki.
entries.4.1: Hearing what Agastya had said, Rama was filled with wonder: how had the rakshasas first come to be in Lanka?
entries.4.2: Then, shaking his head and looking again and again at Agastya, whose form was like the threefold sacrificial fire, he spoke with a smile.
entries.4.3: 'Venerable one, Lanka belonged to the eaters of flesh even before this. Hearing your words, the greatest wonder has come upon me.
entries.4.4: 'We have heard that the rakshasas sprang from the line of Pulastya. But now you have told of their origin from another source as well.
entries.4.5: 'Were they mightier than Ravana, than Kumbhakarna, than Prahasta and Vikata, and than the sons of Ravana?
entries.4.6: 'Who was their forefather, brahmin, and what was the name of that one of surpassing strength? For what offence were they driven out by Vishnu, and how?
entries.4.7: 'Tell me all this in full, sinless one. Dispel this curiosity of mine as the sun dispels the darkness.'
entries.4.8: Hearing Raghava's words, well-formed and auspicious, Agastya was himself a little astonished, and said to him.
entries.4.9: 'Long ago Prajapati, born of the waters, created the waters, and then the lotus-born one created beings to guard them.
entries.4.10: 'Those beings came humbly before their maker, saying "What shall we do?" — for they were afflicted by hunger and thirst and fear.
entries.4.11: 'Prajapati, giver of honour, said to those beings as though smiling, speaking to them with care, "Guard them diligently."
entries.4.12: 'Some among them said "We shall guard," and others said "We shall devour." So the hungry and the not-hungry answered him, and the maker of beings said to them,
entries.4.13: '"Those of you who said 'We shall guard' — let them be rakshasas. And those who said 'We shall devour' — let them be yakshas."
entries.4.14: 'Among them were Heti and Praheti, brothers and lords of the rakshasas, subduers of foes, like Madhu and Kaitabha.
entries.4.15: 'Praheti was righteous and went then to the forest of penance; but Heti made every effort to obtain a wife.
entries.4.16: 'That great-minded one of measureless spirit himself took to wife the sister of Kala, a maiden named Bhaya, terrible to look upon.
entries.4.17: 'Upon her Heti, bull among rakshasas and best of those who have sons, begot a son known as Vidyutkesha.
entries.4.18: 'Vidyutkesha, the son of Heti, was radiant as the blazing sun, and that one of great splendour grew as a cloud grows in the midst of the waters.
entries.4.19: 'When that night-ranger came to the fair time of youth, his father resolved to arrange a marriage for him.
entries.4.20: 'Then Heti, bull among rakshasas, sought for his son the daughter of Sandhya, who was in majesty the equal of Sandhya herself.
entries.4.21: 'Thinking "She must in any case be given to another," Sandhya gave her daughter to Vidyutkesha, Raghava.
entries.4.22: 'Having won Sandhya's daughter, Vidyutkesha the night-ranger took his pleasure with her as Maghavan does with Paulomi.
entries.4.23: 'After some time, Rama, Salakatankata conceived by Vidyutkesha as the ocean conceives the ranks of clouds.
entries.4.24: 'Then that rakshasi went to Mandara and there brought forth a child bright as a laden cloud, as Ganga brought forth the child of Agni.
entries.4.25: 'Having cast the child aside, she who desired only Vidyutkesha's company went back and took her pleasure with her husband, forgetting the son she had borne.
entries.4.26: 'The infant that had been cast away, whose cry was like the sound of thunder and whose radiance was like the autumn sun, put his own fist into his mouth and wept softly.
entries.4.27: 'Then Shiva, mounted upon his bull and accompanied by Parvati, passing along the path of the wind, heard the sound of that weeping.
entries.4.28: 'With Uma he saw the child of the rakshasa weeping; and out of Parvati's compassion Bhava, the destroyer of the three cities,
entries.4.29: 'made that son of a rakshasa equal in years to his own mother. And the great god, imperishable and unchanging, made him deathless as well,
entries.4.30: 'and gave him a city that moved through the sky, to please Parvati. And Uma too, prince, granted a boon to the rakshasas:
entries.4.31: 'that conception should be attained at once, and birth at once, and that the child should at once come to the age of its mother.
entries.4.32: 'Then Sukesha, made proud by the gift of that boon and having received such favour from the side of the lord Hara, ranged everywhere, great and great-minded, as Purandara ranges when he has won his city in the sky.'
entries.4.33: Thus ends the fourth canto of the Uttara Kanda in the Ramayana, the first poem, composed by the sage Valmiki.
entries.5.1: 'Seeing Sukesha righteous and endowed with the boon he had won, a gandharva named Gramani, whose splendour was like that of Vishvavasu,
entries.5.2: 'had a daughter named Devavati, a second Shri, renowned in the three worlds for her beauty and youth; and he gave her in due form to Sukesha, as one gives the very fortune of the rakshasas.
entries.5.3: 'Having gained as her beloved husband one whose lordship came from a boon, Devavati was as glad as a poor man who has come by wealth.
entries.5.4: 'Joined with her, that night-ranger shone as a great elephant shines when it comes forth from a mountain of collyrium with its mate.
entries.5.6: 'he begot three sons whose forms were like the threefold sacrificial fire: Malyavan, Sumali, and Mali the best of the strong. Three sons the lord of rakshasas had, rakshasas equal to the three-eyed god.
entries.5.7: 'They stood like the three worlds untroubled, like the three fires, terrible as the three Vedas, dreadful as the three diseases.
entries.5.8: 'These three sons of Sukesha, blazing like the threefold fire, grew there as maladies grow when they are neglected.
entries.5.9: 'Knowing that their father's boon had come by the power of austerity offered to the lord, the brothers resolved and went to Meru to perform penance.
entries.5.10: 'Taking up dreadful observances, best of kings, those rakshasas practised a terrible austerity that struck fear into all beings.
entries.5.11: 'With penances most hard to bear, joined with truth and uprightness and self-control, they scorched the three worlds together with their gods, asuras and men.
entries.5.12: 'Then the four-faced lord, seated in his excellent chariot, addressed the sons of Sukesha and said, 'I am the giver of boons.'
entries.5.13: 'Knowing Brahma the boon-giver, surrounded by the hosts of the gods with Indra among them, they all spoke with joined palms, trembling like trees.
entries.5.14: '"God, if being propitiated by our austerity you would grant us a boon — that we be unconquerable, slayers of our enemies, and long of life,
entries.5.15: '"that we be mighty, and true to one another."
entries.5.16: 'Saying "So shall it be" to the sons of Sukesha, the lord Brahma, who loves the brahmins, went to the world of Brahma.
entries.5.17: 'Having won that boon, Rama, all those night-rangers then harassed gods and asuras alike, made fearless by the gift.
entries.5.18: 'Assailed by them, the gods with the hosts of sages and charanas could find no protector, like men fallen into hell.
entries.5.19: 'Then the rakshasas came together in gladness, best of the Raghus, and said to Vishvakarma, the imperishable, best of craftsmen:
entries.5.20: '"By your own power you are the builder of houses for the gods, who are great and full of vigour, splendour and strength, and you build what their hearts desire.
entries.5.21: '"Build a house for us also, great-minded one — resting upon Himavat, or upon Meru or Mandara. Make us a great dwelling like the house of Maheshvara."
entries.5.22: 'Then the mighty-armed Vishvakarma told those rakshasas of a dwelling like Shakra's Amaravati.
entries.5.23: '"On the shore of the southern ocean there is a mountain named Trikuta, and there is another beside it, a second, called Suvela, best of beings.
entries.5.24: '"On the middle peak of that mountain, which is like a rain-cloud, hard for even birds to reach, its four sides cut as though with a chisel,
entries.5.25: '"lies a city thirty yojanas broad and a hundred yojanas long, girded with ramparts of gold and encircled with golden archways.
entries.5.26: '"That city Lanka was built by me at Shakra's command. Dwell there, unassailable bulls among rakshasas.
entries.5.27: '"As the dwellers in heaven with Indra among them are secure when they reach Amaravati, so you, surrounded by many rakshasas, on reaching the stronghold of Lanka
entries.5.28: '"shall become unassailable by your foes, destroyers of foes."
entries.5.29: 'Hearing Vishvakarma's words, those best of rakshasas went with a thousand followers and dwelt in that city.
entries.5.30: 'Coming to Lanka with its strong ramparts and moat and its hundreds of golden houses, those night-rangers dwelt there in gladness.
entries.5.31: 'At that same time, Raghava, there was a gandharvi named Narmada who went where she pleased, delight of the Raghus.
entries.5.32: 'She had three daughters, matching in radiance Wisdom, Fortune and Fame. In order of age she gave them, though herself no rakshasi,
entries.5.33: 'she gladly gave those maidens, whose faces were like the full moon — three gandharva maidens to three lords of the rakshasas.
entries.5.34: 'They were given by their mother, those greatly blessed ones, under the constellation of Bhaga. And so the sons of Sukesha were wedded, Rama,
entries.5.35: 'and sported with their wives as the immortals do with the apsaras. Then Malyavan's wife was the beautiful Sundari,
entries.5.36: 'and hear what offspring he begot upon her: Vajramushti, Virupaksha, and the rakshasa Durmukha,
entries.5.37: 'Suptaghna and Yajnakopa, and Matta and Unmatta both; and a daughter Anala was born of the beautiful Sundari, Rama.
entries.5.38: 'Sumali too had a wife whose face was like the full moon, named Ketumati, Rama, dearer to him than life itself.
entries.5.39: 'Hear now in order, great king, what offspring the night-ranger Sumali begot upon Ketumati.
entries.5.40: 'Prahasta, Akampana, Vikata, Kalakarmukha, Dhumraksha, Danda, and the mighty Suparshva,
entries.5.41: 'the rakshasas Samhradi, Praghasa and Bhasakarna; and Raka, Pushpotkata, and Kaikasi of the pure smile, and Kumbhinasi — these are remembered as the offspring of Sumali.
entries.5.43: 'Mali's wife was a gandharvi named Vasudha, graceful of form, with eyes like lotus petals, fair-eyed, like the best of yakshis.
entries.5.44: 'Hear from me, lord, what offspring the younger brother of Sumali begot upon her, Raghava.
entries.5.45: 'Anila, Anala, Hara and Sampati — these night-rangers, sons of Mali, became the ministers of Vibhishana.
entries.5.46: 'Then those three bulls among rakshasas, surrounded by night-rangers and by hundreds of sons, proud of their great valour, harassed the gods with Indra among them, and the sages, nagas and yakshas.
entries.5.47: 'Ranging over the world like the wind, hard to withstand, their splendour in battle the very image of death, grown exceedingly proud through the gift of the boon, they made an end always of the performance of sacrifices.'
entries.5.48: Thus ends the fifth canto of the Uttara Kanda in the Ramayana, the first poem, composed by the sage Valmiki.
